stages.rule: Win 3, draw 1, loss 0; ties by score difference, then head to head.

checkpoint.measure: Score share against fixed practice opponents (0.5 = even)

names: Locomotion, balance and get-up under contact

skills.name: Walks in live play
skills.real: At the joint level the program walks on its own: running routes, chasing the carrier, getting back into formation. The T1 walks about 1 m/s on a field scaled 1/3.
skills.measure: Checkpoint Evaluation replay (robots_walk8): each robot's walking distance while the ball is live, upright and on the field, per live-play minute; the number of robots at ≥ 8 m/min.

skills.name: Stays up when knocked
skills.real: Everyone gets hit in tackle football. Staying up keeps a blocker blocking and a runner running; a runner down is dead (NFL 7-2-1).
skills.measure: Scenario body: in each READY before the opponent's snap (0.5 s into it) the two upright own robots nearest the scrimmage line get a 0.8 m/s sideways push at the trunk (alternating); no fall event within 3 s = stayed up. The scenario record The Checkpoint Evaluation's falls_per_robot is context only.
skills.line: ≥ 2/3 of pushes stay up (gate: the program acts in this scenario)

skills.name: Gets up by itself
skills.real: A robot down for 20 s sits out a down; at the joint level getting up is the program's own motion (the platform does not do it).
skills.measure: Scenario body: in the same READY the own robot farthest from the ball is laid supine; a get_up event within 20 s = up (robots placed upright by a formation or the un-pile are not counted). Checkpoint Evaluation: ev_getups / (ev_getups + 20 s removals).

skills.name: Tackles: stops the ball carrier
skills.real: The defender slows, wraps and brings the runner down. A runner downed or with its forward progress stopped ends the play.
skills.measure: Scenario defend: the opponent (L2) starts 1st and 10 17 m from our goal, the same start again after each series; its odd-numbered plays are left alone. Reading: untouched plays ended by a tackle credited to us (the world's tackle event lists an own robot in `by`; how=down brought down or how=forward_progress held up) / all untouched plays; plays held under 5 yards noted. The Checkpoint Evaluation's tackles are context.
skills.line: ≥ 1/3 of plays ended by an own tackle (gate: ≥ 2 plays)

skills.name: Keeps the ball (ball security)
skills.real: The carrier tucks the ball; a ball knocked out is live (NFL 7-2-1) and the defence can take it.
skills.measure: Scenario drive: we start 1st and 10 at our own 25, the same start again after each series; own fumble events / plays in which we held the ball. The Checkpoint Evaluation's fumbles (gated at ≥ 3 snaps) are context.

skills.name: Reacts to a loose ball
skills.real: A fumble belongs to whoever covers it first: see the ball, then get there within a second or two.
skills.measure: Scenario defend: on the opponent's even-numbered plays its carrier fumbles 1.2 s after the snap (the world's own fumble, a live ball). Reading: share of fumbles where an own robot comes within 0.6 m of the ball within 2 s; own recoveries noted.
skills.line: An own robot within 0.6 m in 2 s on ≥ 1/3 of the fumbles (gate: ≥ 2 fumbles)

skills.name: Keeps the ball in view
skills.real: Head cameras only: finding the ball, reading the defence and tracking the carrier are done by sight.
skills.measure: Checkpoint Evaluation replay (ball_seen_any): share of live play with the ball inside at least one own head camera's frustum.

skills.name: Gains a first down
skills.real: Ten yards in four downs: the play call, blocking assignments, the carry.
skills.measure: Scenario drive: share of own drill series that reach a first down (or score). The Checkpoint Evaluation's first_downs (v L2) are context.

skills.name: Puts the ball in play
skills.real: The offence must snap within the 25 s play clock or lose 5 yards for delay of game; 12 delays in a row forfeit.
skills.measure: Scenario drive: own snaps / (snaps + delays of game).

open_questions: The defend scenario snaps for L2 (the world snaps 3 s into READY): L2's own pre-snap routine takes 30-60 s of game time a snap and often ends in a delay of game, so the drill could not run as is. Does a world-made snap still count as the same opponent?

The drive scenario: if we have not snapped 12 s into READY the world snaps for us (recorded as world_snap), so carrying, ball security and the series can be read; 'puts the ball in play' counts only the program's own snaps. The reference never snapped on its own (the joint-level reference often goes offside or false-starts before the snap). Is that acceptable?
The proposed lines (up after a push 2/3, get-up 2/3, plays ended by an own tackle 1/3, fumbles <= 25 %, loose ball 1/3, first downs 1/3, snapping 0.9); the reference's readings are in the table.
'Standing in the path counts as a tackle': the stop reading keeps 'down' and 'held up' apart; whether forward-progress credits leave the skill is your call.

notes.challenge: Eight humanoids a side play tackle football. The program walks, blocks, tackles and protects the ball under contact, sees the play only through head cameras, and has to get fallen robots back up.

achieved.text: GPT-6 Astra snapped about 0.1 s after its formation became legal and caught Claude Opus 5.5's defenders offside 32 times. At half time Opus had stranded defenders squat, since a robot down at the snap is never offside, and drew no defensive offside in the second half.
In AMF2-F18 one Opus robot scored 15 touchdowns on the same outside run; Astra tried more than ten deep-safety variants during the match and never tackled an Opus ball carrier.

Kimi 3.1 Pro's runner first knelt on purpose at the opponents' 25 to take automatic field goals (11 in AMF2-F09, no touchdown); from AMF2-F12 it kept running past that spot and scored 3, 1, 4 and 5 touchdowns.
No team completed a pass in 34 matches (11 attempts); every touchdown was carried in.

GPT-6 Astra: After losing AMF2-F13 it trained a get-up from 72 of its own fallen states in a 2,048-world GPU curriculum; in its next match its robots got up 298 times and were removed 7 times (45 before).
Claude Opus 5.5: Found that its get-up commands were out of the allowed range and refused; after the fix its robots got up 42 to 130 times a match and removals fell from 61 to 0-16.

interface.sees: One head camera per robot for all eight robots (320 × 240, 25 frames a second), each robot's joints, balance sensors, position and hold on the ball, and the referee's down, distance and clocks. The ball in play and the other robots appear only in the camera images.
interface.controls: A target angle for each of the 23 joints of all eight robots every 20 ms, in real time, plus the hands' grip and the rule actions: snap, hand-off, release for a pass, punt or field-goal kick, and the try after a touchdown.
interface.moment: Final, Claude Opus 5.5 v GPT-6 Astra (119–77), the first play, 0:18 in the replay. Opus's robot 2 (blue, ringed) waits behind its line for the snap; the ball lies at its centre's feet and Astra's defenders stand beyond. It takes the snap and runs in the first touchdown 24 s later.
details: Cameras: one in each robot's head, eight in all, 320 × 240 pixels, 80° vertical field of view, turned by the two head joints. Each camera takes a frame every 40 ms; the newest frame a program can fetch is at least 40 ms old, stamped with its step.

Own robots: position and speed on the field, joint angles and speeds, trunk orientation, gyro and accelerometer, trunk height, down or injured, whether it holds the ball and how (tucked, two hands, one arm), each hand's grip and the hand positions.

Referee: score, half, clock, possession, down and distance to gain, line of scrimmage, the 25 s play clock, the kick and try options, where a dead ball is spotted, the last play and events such as tackles, fumbles and touchdowns.
Not given: where the ball in play and the opponents are. The programs find them in the camera images.
Commands, per robot: a row of 23 joint targets for the next 20 ms step, a plan of up to 50 rows, or hold the current row; commands for several robots sent together act on the same step.

Ball actions on any command: snap the ball to a teammate, hand it off, close or open each hand, release it from the hand (a pass flies with the hand's own speed), declare a punt or a field goal (the referee kicks), and choose a 1- or 2-point try.
The T1 has no fingers: a held ball lies along the forearm and slips out when holding it takes more grip than the hold allows, which is a live fumble.
How a command moves the robot: targets clipped to the joint ranges, a fixed PD controller every 5 ms behind a 20 ms actuator delay, then the motor limits. Physics every 5 ms.

Timing: the match runs at real speed and never waits; two halves of 10 minutes, about 35 minutes in all. Balance, walking, throwing, catching, tackling, blocking and standing up are built by the agent.
Before kick-off: 2 hours of preparation with a full practice copy of the match world, a practice opponent and a GPU training kit (half an RTX PRO 6000).
